passages.title: The box that changed the world
paras: Almost everything we buy, from clothes and televisions to bananas and car parts, has spent part of its journey inside a steel box. The shipping container, a simple metal case of standard size, is one of the least glamorous inventions of the twentieth century. Yet many economists believe it did more to create today’s global economy than any trade agreement.

Before containers, cargo was loaded onto ships in much the same way as it had been for centuries. Goods arrived at the port in sacks, barrels and wooden crates of every shape and size, and teams of dock workers carried them onto the ship one by one. This process, known as break-bulk shipping, was extremely slow. A typical cargo ship could spend as long in port being loaded and unloaded as it did at sea. It was also expensive: in the 1950s, loading and unloading could account for half the total cost of transporting goods across the ocean.

Theft was another problem. With so many items passing through so many hands, goods regularly disappeared at the docks. Some port workers were said to treat a share of the cargo as an unofficial part of their wages, and companies shipping valuable products such as whisky or cigarettes expected to lose a percentage of every load.

The man usually credited with changing all this is Malcom McLean, an American who owned a trucking company. According to the most popular version of the story, McLean had the idea in 1937, while waiting for hours at a port as his cotton was loaded onto a ship. It was not until 1956, however, that he put the idea into practice. He bought an old tanker, strengthened its deck, and sent it from New Jersey to Texas carrying 58 metal boxes that had previously been the trailers of trucks.

McLean’s real insight was not the box itself. Others had experimented with containers before him. What he understood was that the container was only valuable as part of a complete system. Ships, ports, cranes, trucks and trains all had to be designed around the same box, so that it could be moved from one form of transport to another without ever being opened. This idea is known as intermodal transport.

For this system to work internationally, containers had to be the same size everywhere. In the 1960s, after years of difficult negotiations, the International Organization for Standardization agreed on standard dimensions. The most common container today is twenty or forty feet long and eight feet wide, and the corners are fitted with special metal fittings that allow cranes to lift them and lock them together.

The effects were dramatic. Ships could now be loaded in hours rather than days, and the cost of loading cargo fell by more than ninety per cent. Because goods were sealed inside the box from factory to destination, theft fell sharply, and insurance costs fell with it. Ships became much larger: the biggest modern container ships can carry more than twenty thousand containers at once.

Not everyone benefited. Thousands of dock workers lost their jobs, as a few crane operators could now do the work of hundreds of men. Traditional ports in city centres, such as those in London and New York, declined because they had no space for the huge storage areas that containers required, and new ports were built elsewhere. Many old dockland areas were later turned into offices and housing.

The container also changed the ships themselves. Early container ships were converted cargo vessels, but by the 1970s shipyards were building vessels designed specifically to carry boxes, with deep holds divided into vertical cells into which containers could be dropped by crane. Containers were also stacked high on deck, held in place by steel bars. Because such ships spent so little time in port, shipping companies could run regular, reliable timetables, which in turn allowed manufacturers to plan production with much greater confidence. A factory could now order parts from another continent, knowing almost exactly when they would arrive.

Above all, the container made it possible for companies to produce goods wherever costs were lowest and ship them anywhere in the world cheaply. Today, the cost of shipping is so small that it adds only a few cents to the price of a pair of shoes made on the other side of the world.

passages.title: How do birds find their way?
paras: Every autumn, billions of birds leave their breeding grounds and fly thousands of kilometres to spend the winter in warmer regions. Some, such as the Arctic tern, travel from one end of the planet to the other. Even more remarkably, many birds return to exactly the same nest the following spring. How they manage to find their way has puzzled scientists for centuries, and although much has been learned, the full answer is still not known.

The first scientific clues came from experiments with captive birds in the 1950s. The German ornithologist Gustav Kramer noticed that caged starlings became restless during the migration season and tended to face in the direction they would normally fly. When he used mirrors to change the apparent position of the sun, the birds changed direction accordingly. This showed that they were using the sun as a compass. Since the sun moves across the sky during the day, this also meant that the birds must have an internal clock that allowed them to adjust for the time.

Many birds, however, migrate at night. In the 1960s, researchers placed young birds in a planetarium, where the night sky could be controlled. They found that the birds learned to recognise the point in the sky around which the stars appeared to rotate. In the northern hemisphere, this point is close to the Pole Star, and it indicates north. Interestingly, the birds were not born with knowledge of particular star patterns; they had to learn them while young.

Birds can navigate even when the sky is completely covered by cloud, which suggests that they also have a magnetic sense. Experiments in which magnets were attached to pigeons showed that their ability to find their way home was disturbed on cloudy days, although not on sunny ones. For a long time, it was thought that tiny particles of iron in birds’ beaks acted as a kind of compass needle. More recent research, however, points to a different explanation: special molecules in the eye that react to the Earth’s magnetic field, possibly allowing birds to actually see magnetic lines as a pattern over their normal vision.

A compass alone, however, is not enough. To reach a specific destination, a bird also needs to know where it is, in the same way that a sailor needs both a compass and a map. There is growing evidence that some birds use smell for this purpose. When researchers blocked the sense of smell of seabirds and released them far out at sea, the birds were unable to find their way back to their colonies, whereas birds whose sense of smell was not affected returned without difficulty.

Young birds face a particular challenge. Many species migrate alone in their first year, without parents to guide them, and yet they head in the right direction. This suggests that the basic direction and distance of the journey are inherited. In one famous experiment, scientists caught young birds in the Netherlands and released them in Switzerland. The young birds continued in the same direction they would have taken from the Netherlands and ended up in the wrong place. Adult birds, by contrast, corrected their course and reached their usual wintering areas, showing that experience allows them to build a more detailed map.

Technology has transformed the study of migration in recent years. Until quite recently, the only way to follow a bird was to put a small metal ring on its leg and hope that someone would find it later, which happened in only a tiny proportion of cases. Today, tracking devices weighing less than a gram can record a bird’s position for months, and some can send data by satellite. These devices have revealed journeys that nobody suspected: one small songbird was found to fly non-stop over the Atlantic for three days, while some birds were shown to take completely different routes in spring and autumn.

Understanding migration has practical importance. Many migratory bird populations are declining, partly because of the loss of the wetlands and forests where they stop to rest and feed during their journeys. Bright city lights also confuse birds flying at night, causing millions of deaths each year from collisions with buildings. Some cities now switch off unnecessary lights during the main migration seasons, a simple measure that has been shown to save many lives.

passages.title: Should handwriting survive?
paras: In many schools around the world, handwriting is quietly disappearing. Children who learn to type on tablets from an early age may write by hand only occasionally, and some education systems have reduced the time spent teaching joined-up writing or dropped it altogether. To many people this seems a sensible response to a changing world. Why spend hours practising a skill that adults rarely use? I want to argue that this view is mistaken, and that we abandon handwriting at our cost.

The most important argument concerns learning. A number of studies have compared students who take notes by hand with those who type them. Typists record more words, which might seem an advantage. But because they can type almost as fast as a lecturer speaks, they tend to copy what they hear word for word. Students writing by hand cannot do this; they are forced to select, summarise and put ideas into their own words. When tested later, the handwriters generally show a better understanding of the material, although the difference in their ability to remember simple facts is small.

Research on young children points in the same direction. In one study, children who practised writing letters by hand were better at recognising them later than children who practised by typing or tracing. Brain scans showed that writing by hand activated areas associated with reading in a way that typing did not. The physical effort of forming each letter, it seems, helps the brain to learn its shape.

Supporters of digital learning reply that these studies are small and that technology is changing fast. They point out that styluses now allow students to write on screens, combining the benefits of handwriting with the convenience of digital storage. This is a fair point, and I see no reason why handwriting must take place on paper. What matters is the act of forming letters, not the material used.

Another common objection is that time is limited and that schools should focus on skills that will be needed in the workplace. It is certainly true that most adults type far more than they write. But this argument misunderstands the purpose of teaching handwriting to young children. The aim is not to produce adults who write long documents by hand; it is to support the development of reading, spelling and fine motor control, which are needed whatever technology people later use.

There is also the question of fairness. Not every child has a computer at home, and exams in many countries are still taken on paper. Children who have had little practice in writing by hand may be at a disadvantage when they must write quickly for two or three hours. Until exam systems change, I believe it would be irresponsible to stop teaching handwriting properly.

None of this means that we should return to the strict handwriting lessons of the past, when children were punished for untidy letters and left-handed pupils were forced to use their right hand. Beautiful handwriting is not the goal. Clear, fluent writing that does not require conscious effort is, because only then can a child concentrate on what they want to say rather than on how to form the letters.

It is worth adding that handwriting has value outside the classroom. Many adults say that they think more clearly when they plan with a pen, and writers, designers and scientists often begin their work with rough sketches and notes. A handwritten letter or card also carries a personal meaning that a typed message rarely does. These benefits are harder to measure than test scores, but they are not imaginary, and they are another reason to make sure that every child leaves school able to write comfortably.

Technology will continue to change the way we communicate, and it would be foolish to resist that. But the evidence suggests that the hand and the brain are more closely connected than we once thought. A skill that has served people for five thousand years deserves more careful thought before it is abandoned.
